claim: Biological clocks have been developed at different molecular levels and were found to be more advanced in the presence of somatic illness and mental disorders.
source: Biological clocks have been developed at different molecular levels and were found to be more advanced in the presence of somatic illness and mental disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that references established knowledge in the field without specific data from this study.

claim: Correlations between biological aging indicators were small (all r < 0.2).
source: Correlations between biological aging indicators were small (all r < 0.2), indicating little overlap.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing correlation coefficients.

claim: The most consistent associations of advanced biological aging were found for male sex, higher body mass index (BMI), metabolic syndrome, smoking, and depression.
source: The most consistent associations of advanced biological aging were found for male sex, higher body mass index (BMI), metabolic syndrome, smoking, and depression.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings from the association analyses presented in the results.

claim: A composite index of all five clocks showed most pronounced associations with health determinants compared to individual clocks.
source: As compared to the individual clocks, a composite index of all five clocks showed most pronounced associations with health determinants.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis data presented in the results section.

claim: One's biological age is best reflected by combining aging measures from multiple cellular levels.
source: The large effect sizes of the composite index and the low correlation between biological aging indicators suggest that one's biological age is best reflected by combining aging measures from multiple cellular levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing low correlations and larger effect sizes for the composite index.

claim: Biological aging can be estimated by various cellular indices.
source: Biological aging can be estimated by various cellular indices (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Commonly used indices are based on telomere length, DNA methylation patterns (epigenetic age), variation in transcription (transcriptomic age) as well as alterations in the metabolome (metabolomic age) and in the proteome (proteomic age).
source: Commonly used indices are based on telomere length, DNA methylation patterns (epigenetic age), variation in transcription (transcriptomic age) as well as alterations in the metabolome (metabolomic age) and in the proteome (proteomic age) (see Han et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2017 and Jylhävä et al., 2017 for recent reviews).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Biological aging is defined as the residuals of regressing predicted biological age on chronological age: a positive value indicates that the biological age is larger than the chronological age.
source: Biological aging is defined as the residuals of regressing predicted biological age on chronological age: a positive value indicates that the biological age is larger than the chronological age.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: Advanced biological aging has been associated to poor somatic health, including the onset of aging-related somatic diseases such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cognitive decline.
source: Advanced biological aging (i.e. an increased biological clock) has been associated to poor somatic health, including the onset of aging-related somatic diseases such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cognitive decline (Xia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Advanced biological aging has been correlated to mental health: childhood trauma, psychological stress, and psychiatric disorders.
source: Advanced biological aging has also been correlated to mental health: childhood trauma (Li et al., 2017), psychological stress, and psychiatric disorders (Darrow et al., 2016; Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Telomere length has been found to be shorter in various somatic conditions.
source: Specifically, telomere length has been most extensively researched and was found to be shorter in various somatic conditions (Jin et al., 2018), all-cause mortality (Mons et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018) and a range of psychiatric disorders (Lindqvist et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Advanced epigenetic aging has been linked to worse somatic health and mortality.
source: Advanced epigenetic aging has also been linked to worse somatic health, mortality (Marioni et al., 2015), depressive disorder (Han et al., 2018; Whalley, 2017), and post-traumatic stress disorder (Wolf et al., 2018), although some studies have found associations with the opposite direction of effect (Verhoeven et al., 2018; Boks et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Advanced transcriptomic aging was found in those with higher blood pressure, cholesterol levels, fasting glucose, and body mass index (BMI).
source: Advanced transcriptomic aging was found in those with higher blood pressure, cholesterol levels, fasting glucose, and body mass index (BMI) (Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Advanced metabolomic aging increases risk on future cardiovascular disease, mortality, and functionality.
source: Advanced metabolomic aging increases risk on future cardiovascular disease, mortality, and functionality (Akker et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Belsky and colleagues recently showed low agreement between eleven quantifications of biological aging including telomere length, epigenetic aging, and biomarker-composites.
source: Belsky and colleagues (Belsky et al., 2017) recently showed low agreement between eleven quantifications of biological aging including telomere length, epigenetic aging, and biomarker-composites.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Hastings et al., 2019 showed relatively strong correlations (r > 0.50) between three physiological composite biological clocks, but not with telomere length.
source: In contrast, Hastings et al., 2019 showed relatively strong correlations (r > 0.50) between three physiological composite biological clocks (i.e. homeostatic dysregulation, Klemer and Doubal's method and Levine's method), but not with telomere length.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Telomere length was not correlated with epigenetic aging.
source: Other studies showed that telomere length was not correlated with epigenetic aging (Han et al., 2018; Marioni et al., 2018), although cell type composition adjustments revealed a modest association (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both Hannum and Horvath epigenetic clocks showed modest correlations to a transcriptomic clock.
source: Further, both Hannum and Horvath epigenetic clocks (Hannum et al., 2013; Horvath et al., 2012) showed modest correlations to a transcriptomic clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is unlikely that a single biological clock can fully capture the complexity of the aging process.
source: As it is unlikely that a single biological clock can fully capture the complexity of the aging process (Cole et al., 2019), a composite index, that integrates the different biological clocks and thereby aging at several molecular levels, may reveal the strongest health impact.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a hypothesis.

claim: The study examined approximately 3000 subjects.
source: In ~3000 subjects, we examined whether five biological clocks (telomere length, epigenetic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic clocks) were interrelated and associated to somatic and mental health determinants.
evidence: This is a description of the study design and sample size.

claim: Correlations between chronological age and predicted biological age were 0.30 for telomere length, 0.95 for epigenetic age, 0.72 for transcriptomic age, 0.85 for proteomic age, and 0.70 for metabolomic age.
source: Correlations between chronological age and predicted biological age were 0.30 for telomere length, 0.95 for epigenetic age, 0.72 for transcriptomic age, 0.85 for proteomic age, and 0.70 for metabolomic age (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: Correlations between biological aging indicators were significant for 3 out of 10 pairs: proteomic vs metabolomic aging (r = 0.19, p=2e-16), transcriptomic vs epigenetic aging (r = 0.15, p=3e-06) and transcriptomic vs proteomic aging (r = 0.08, p=2e-06).
source: Correlations were significant for 3 out of 10 pairs; proteomic vs metabolomic aging (r = 0.19, p=2e-16), transcriptomic vs epigenetic aging (r = 0.15, p=3e-06) and transcriptomic vs proteomic aging (r = 0.08, p=2e-06).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Women were biologically younger than men for telomere length (p=3e-4), epigenetic aging (p=5e-4), transcriptomic aging (p=4e-11), and metabolomic aging (p=1e-5).
source: Except for proteomic aging, sex was associated with all biological aging indicators: women were biologically younger than men (p=3e-4 for telomere length, p=5e-4 for epigenetic aging, p=4e-11 for transcriptomic aging, p=1e-5 for metabolomic aging).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Education was not associated with any biological aging indicator.
source: Education was not associated with any biological aging indicator.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Alcohol use was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=3e-3).
source: Among the lifestyle determinants, alcohol use was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=3e-3) and smoking (packs per year) was associated with shorter telomere length (p=3e-3), and advanced transcriptomic (p=2e-2), proteomic (p=1e-5) and metabolomic aging (p=5e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Smoking was associated with shorter telomere length (p=3e-3), and advanced transcriptomic (p=2e-2), proteomic (p=1e-5) and metabolomic aging (p=5e-3).
source: Among the lifestyle determinants, alcohol use was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=3e-3) and smoking (packs per year) was associated with shorter telomere length (p=3e-3), and advanced transcriptomic (p=2e-2), proteomic (p=1e-5) and metabolomic aging (p=5e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Physical activity was not associated with any biological aging indicator.
source: Physical activity was not associated with any biological aging indicator.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: High BMI was strongly associated with advanced biological aging of all indicators (p=2e-2 for telomere length, p=4e-3 for epigenetic aging, p=6e-10 for transcriptomic aging, p=1e-7 for proteomic aging, and p=2e-35 for metabolomic aging).
source: From the somatic health determinants, high BMI was strongly associated with advanced biological aging of all indicators (p=2e-2 for telomere length, p=4e-3 for epigenetic aging, p=6e-10 for transcriptomic aging, p=1e-7 for proteomic aging, and p=2e-35 for metabolomic aging).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Physical disability was associated with advanced epigenetic aging (p=1e-4).
source: Physical disability was associated with advanced epigenetic aging (p=1e-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The presence of digestive diseases was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=2e-2).
source: Within the domain of chronic diseases, the presence of digestive diseases and endocrine diseases were associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=2e-2 and p=1e-2, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The presence of endocrine diseases was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=1e-2).
source: Within the domain of chronic diseases, the presence of digestive diseases and endocrine diseases were associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=2e-2 and p=1e-2, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Subjects with cardiometabolic disease showed advanced metabolomic aging (p=4e-3).
source: Subjects with cardiometabolic disease showed advanced metabolomic aging (p=4e-3) and subjects with digestive disease exhibited advanced transcriptomic aging (p=1e-2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Subjects with digestive disease exhibited advanced transcriptomic aging (p=1e-2).
source: Subjects with cardiometabolic disease showed advanced metabolomic aging (p=4e-3) and subjects with digestive disease exhibited advanced transcriptomic aging (p=1e-2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Those with metabolic syndrome showed advanced biological aging across four indicators (p=6e-4 for telomere length, p=1e-8 for transcriptomic aging, p=5e-9 for proteomic aging, p=5e-29 for metabolomic aging).
source: Those with metabolic syndrome showed advanced biological aging across four indicators (p=6e-4 for telomere length, p=1e-8 for transcriptomic aging, p=5e-9 for proteomic aging, p=5e-29 for metabolomic aging).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The presence of current depression was associated with advanced epigenetic aging (p=2e-3).
source: The presence of current depression and depression severity were associated advanced epigenetic (p=2e-3 and p=9e-5) and proteomic aging (p=8e-3 and p=6e-3, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Depression severity was associated with advanced epigenetic aging (p=9e-5).
source: The presence of current depression and depression severity were associated advanced epigenetic (p=2e-3 and p=9e-5) and proteomic aging (p=8e-3 and p=6e-3, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The presence of current depression was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=8e-3).
source: The presence of current depression and depression severity were associated advanced epigenetic (p=2e-3 and p=9e-5) and proteomic aging (p=8e-3 and p=6e-3, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Depression severity was associated with advanced proteomic aging (p=6e-3).
source: The presence of current depression and depression severity were associated advanced epigenetic (p=2e-3 and p=9e-5) and proteomic aging (p=8e-3 and p=6e-3, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Current depression was associated with advanced transcriptomic aging (p=2e-2).
source: Current depression was also associated with advanced transcriptomic aging (p=2e-2) and those with childhood trauma showed advanced epigenetic aging (p=8e-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Those with childhood trauma showed advanced epigenetic aging (p=8e-5).
source: Current depression was also associated with advanced transcriptomic aging (p=2e-2) and those with childhood trauma showed advanced epigenetic aging (p=8e-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Metabolomic aging was associated with the increased use of metabolic medication (Beta = 0.153, p=2.35e-3).
source: After FDR correction, we found that metabolomic aging was associated with the increased use of metabolic medication (Beta = 0.153, p=2.35e-3), and antidepressant use with proteomic (Beta = 0.208, p=7.16e-5) and transcriptomic aging (Beta = 0.129, p=8.1e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Antidepressant use was associated with proteomic aging (Beta = 0.208, p=7.16e-5).
source: After FDR correction, we found that metabolomic aging was associated with the increased use of metabolic medication (Beta = 0.153, p=2.35e-3), and antidepressant use with proteomic (Beta = 0.208, p=7.16e-5) and transcriptomic aging (Beta = 0.129, p=8.1e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Antidepressant use was associated with transcriptomic aging (Beta = 0.129, p=8.1e-3).
source: After FDR correction, we found that metabolomic aging was associated with the increased use of metabolic medication (Beta = 0.153, p=2.35e-3), and antidepressant use with proteomic (Beta = 0.208, p=7.16e-5) and transcriptomic aging (Beta = 0.129, p=8.1e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: There were no significant associations between chronic disease onset or mortality and baseline biological aging.
source: There were no significant associations between chronic disease onset or mortality and baseline biological aging, likely due to the low numbers of mortality and disease onset (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The composite index was computed as the sum of the five scaled biological aging indicators in the 653 samples with data of all five biological levels.
source: The composite index was computed as the sum of the five scaled biological aging indicators in the 653 samples with data of all five biological levels.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used to create the composite index.

claim: Correlations between the five biological aging indicators and the composite index were between 0.43 and 0.51.
source: Correlations between the five biological aging indicators and the composite index were between 0.43 and 0.51.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data.

claim: The composite index showed associations with sex (p=2e-6), BMI (p=2e-10), smoking (p=2e-2), metabolic syndrome (p=9e-13), current MDD (p=6e-3), depression severity (p=7e-4), and childhood trauma (p=2e-2).
source: We found more and stronger associations for the composite index than for any of the individual biological aging indicators: including sex (p=2e-6), BMI (p=2e-10), smoking (p=2e-2), metabolic syndrome (p=9e-13), current MDD (p=6e-3), depression severity (p=7e-4), and childhood trauma (p=2e-2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The first principle component (PC) of PCA was a weighted sum of the biological aging indicators (for telomere length the weight (w) = 0.042, epigenetic aging w = 0.094, transcriptomic aging w = 0.220, proteomic aging w = 0.707, metabolomic aging w = 0.664).
source: We used the first principle component (PC) of this analysis, which was a weighted sum of the biological aging indicators (for telomere length the weight (w) = 0.042, epigenetic aging w = 0.094, transcriptomic aging w = 0.220, proteomic aging w = 0.707, metabolomic aging w = 0.664), reflecting the highest correlations between the biological aging indicators, which is between metabolomic and proteomic aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The five PCs each explain more than 15% of variance (the first 2 PCs more than 25% each).
source: The five PC's each explain more than 15% of variance (the first 2 PC's more than 25% each), indicating the multidimensionality and non-redundancy of the five biological aging indicators.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Male sex, high BMI, smoking, and metabolic syndrome were consistently associated with more advanced levels of biological aging across at least four of the biological clocks.
source: Separate linear regressions showed that male sex, high BMI, smoking, and metabolic syndrome were consistently associated with more advanced levels of biological aging across at least four of the biological clocks.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the association analyses.

claim: Depression was associated to more advanced levels of epigenetic, transcriptomic and proteomic aging.
source: Strikingly, depression was associated to more advanced levels of epigenetic, transcriptomic and proteomic aging, signifying that both somatic and mental health are associated with advanced biological aging.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the association analyses.

claim: The range of correlations among the biological aging indicators indicates that the correlates of chronological age in different molecular layers were not strongly correlated.
source: The range of correlations among the biological aging indicators considered in this study indicates that the correlates of chronological age in different molecular layers were not strongly correlated, suggesting that biological aging may be differently manifested at certain cellular levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data presented in the results.

claim: The correlation between metabolomic and proteomic aging may partly be explained by the fact that both data were obtained from platforms that were aimed at probing central inflammation lipid processes.
source: The correlation between metabolomic and proteomic aging may partly be explained by the fact that both data were obtained from platforms that were aimed at probing central inflammation lipid processes, rather than the full proteome or metabolome.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed correlation.

claim: Male sex was associated with shorter telomere length and advanced epigenetic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic aging, in line with a large body of literature that shows advanced biological aging and earlier mortality in males compared to females.
source: First, male sex was associated with shorter telomere length and advanced epigenetic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic aging, in line with a large body of literature that shows advanced biological aging and earlier mortality in males compared to females (Austad and Fischer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to prior literature.

claim: High BMI was consistently related to all biological aging indicators.
source: Second, high BMI was consistently related to all biological aging indicators, showing that the more overweight or obese, the higher the biological age (Gielen et al., 2018), also after controlling for sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Earlier studies showed similar associations between high BMI and shorter telomere length.
source: Earlier studies showed similar associations between high BMI and shorter telomere length (Gielen et al., 2018), and older epigenetic (Horvath and Raj, 2018) and transcriptomic aging signatures (Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The prevalence of metabolic syndrome was associated with advanced levels of aging.
source: Third, our analyses showed similarly consistent associations between the prevalence of metabolic syndrome and advanced levels of aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: All but epigenetic aging was advanced with respect to cigarette smoking.
source: Further, all but epigenetic aging was advanced with respect to cigarette smoking.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Major depressive disorder (MDD) status was consistently related to advanced aging in three (epigenetic, transcriptomic, proteomic) out of the five biological aging indicators.
source: Major depressive disorder (MDD) status was consistently related to advanced aging in three (epigenetic, transcriptomic, proteomic) out of the five biological aging indicators.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: A recent study (N > 1000) in young adults (20–39 years) did not show associations between mental health and biological aging.
source: In contrast, a recent study (N > 1000) in young adults (20–39 years) did not show associations between mental health (as measured by the CIDI) and biological aging (indicated by telomere length, homeostatic dysregulation, Klemer and Doubal's method and Levine's method) (Hastings et al., 2019), but it seems possible that this sample was too young to fully develop aging-related manifestations of mental health problems, or lacked age variation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and includes speculation about the reasons for the null finding.

claim: The composite index demonstrates larger effect sizes for BMI, sex, smoking, depression severity, and metabolic syndrome than the individual aging indicators.
source: Given that this composite index demonstrates larger effect sizes for BMI, sex, smoking, depression severity, and metabolic syndrome than the individual aging indicators, it is suggested that being biologically old at multiple cellular levels has a cumulative multi-systemic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis data and includes an inference about cumulative effects.

claim: The proteomic and metabolomic clocks mostly measure inflammatory or metabolic factors.
source: Part of this answer requires discussion on the features used to build the different clocks: the proteomic and metabolomic clocks mostly measure inflammatory or metabolic factors, two highly integrated processes in aging and aging-related diseases (Frasca et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a description of the methodology and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies suggest immune-mediated mechanisms (specifically inflammatory signaling) connecting metabolic syndrome, mental health disorders, and aging.
source: Previous studies suggest immune-mediated mechanisms (specifically inflammatory signaling) connecting metabolic syndrome (Révész et al., 2015), mental health disorders (Wohleb et al., 2016), and aging (Révész et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MDD is a condition in which inflammation, obesity, and premature or advanced aging co-occur and converge.
source: Moreover, MDD is a condition in which inflammation, obesity, and premature or advanced aging co-occur and converge.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Immunity and 'inflammaging' may tie together the currently observed associations.
source: It might therefore be speculated that immunity and 'inflammaging' (Franceschi et al., 2018) may tie together the currently observed associations.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Generated omics data are platform-dependent.
source: First and foremost, generated omics data are platform-dependent and the existing epigenetic (Horvath, 2013) and gene expression (Peters et al., 2015) clocks rely on arrays with different coverage of probes as was used in NESDA, that also target different parts of genes.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about omics data and is supported by citations.

claim: A subsample of NESDA was part of the previously published metabolomic clock.
source: Second, a subsample of NESDA was part of the previously published metabolomic clock (Akker et al., 2019), thus application of this model to the current dataset would result in overfitting.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and data overlap with prior work.

claim: The current proteomic platform has not been used before to train a biological clock.
source: The current proteomic platform has not been used before to train a biological clock.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the methodology.

claim: There is currently no validated gold standard for calculating transcriptomic, proteomic, or metabolomic clocks.
source: Moreover, there is currently no validated gold standard for calculating transcriptomic, proteomic, or metabolomic clocks.
evidence: This represents current knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: The approach used for training biological clocks relies on the assumption that the determined cross-sectional correlation between the omics patterns and chronological age arise mainly as a consequence of biological aging, and is independent from potential secular trends.
source: This approach relies on the assumption that the determined cross-sectional correlation between the omics patterns and chronological age arise mainly as a consequence of biological aging, and is independent from potential secular trends (Nelson et al., 2020; Belsky, 2015; Belsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological assumption supported by citations.

claim: It is impossible to completely rule out potential cohort effects or uncontrolled individual differences in cross-sectional studies.
source: As common to cross-sectional studies, it is, however, impossible to completely rule out potential cohort effects or uncontrolled individual differences and results should be interpreted in light of this limitation.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about limitations of cross-sectional study designs.

claim: Other epigenetic clocks exist that are trained to predict other potential criteria such as phenotypic markers of age (DNAm PhenoAge) or a composite biomarker (GrimAge).
source: While the current study only used chronological age as criterion endpoint, it is important to mention that other epigenetic clocks exist that are trained to predict other potential criteria such as phenotypic markers of age (DNAm PhenoAge) (Levine et al., 2018) or a composite biomarker that was derived from DNAm surrogates and smoking in pack-years (GrimAge) (Hillary et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Such clocks were developed to lead to improved predictions of risk of mortality.
source: Such clocks were developed to lead to improved predictions of risk of mortality.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the purpose of alternative epigenetic clocks.

claim: Dysregulation of immunoinflammatory control may be related to metabolic outcomes, aging, and depression.
source: Yet, it could conceivably be hypothesized that dysregulation of immunoinflammatory control may be related to metabolic outcomes, aging, and depression (Diniz and Vieira, 2018), providing scope as to why some of these determinants converge across different platforms and multiple biological levels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: The study used a large cohort that was well-characterized in terms of demographics, lifestyle, and both somatic and mental health assessments.
source: Here, we used a large cohort that was well-characterized in terms of demographics, lifestyle, and both somatic and mental health assessments, to study and integrate five biological clocks across multiple levels of analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the study design and strengths.

claim: The sample was adequately powered to detect statistically significant associations.
source: Moreover, our sample was adequately powered to detect statistically significant associations, limiting the possibility for chance findings and increasing probability for identifying robust biological age determinants.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical power of the study.

claim: The cross-sectional nature of the study prevents drawing conclusions on whether the determinants accelerate the aging trajectory over time.
source: On the other hand, an obvious limitation is the cross-sectional nature of this study that prevents us from drawing any conclusions on whether the determinants accelerate the aging trajectory over time, the other way around, or whether 'third' variables effect this association.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study design.

claim: The relatively young age of the current sample limits the interpretability of findings in the context of increased risk of developing aging-related diseases and mortality.
source: Another aspect that limits the interpretability of our findings in the context of increased risk of developing aging-related diseases and mortality was the relatively young age of the current sample.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study sample.

claim: Previous studies that have associated biological aging with mortality risk commonly include aging cohorts.
source: Previous studies that have associated biological aging with mortality risk commonly include aging cohorts (Danish longitudinal twin study with mean age of 86.1 years; Framingham Offspring Study with mean age 61.0 years; Swedish population cohort SATSA with mean age 63.6 years; German population cohort ESTHER with mean age 62.5 years; Lothian Birth Cohorts with mean age >69.5 years; Normative Aging Study with mean age 71.7 years) (Marioni et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Christiansen et al., 2016; Perna et al., 2016; Murabito et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Before definitively interpreting a 'clock' as a measure of biological aging, further independent studies are needed to establish that the clock changes with advancing age and forecasts disease, disability and mortality.
source: Before definitively interpreting a 'clock' as a measure of biological aging, further independent studies are needed to establish that the clock changes with advancing age and forecasts disease, disability and mortality.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research to validate biological clocks.

claim: The findings indicate that biological aging indicators largely track distinct, but also partially overlapping aspects of the aging process.
source: Our findings indicate that they largely track distinct, but also partially overlapping aspects of this aging process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation data.

claim: The study contributes to the understanding and identification of biological age determinants.
source: Taken together, our findings contribute to the understanding and identification of biological age determinants, important to the development of end points for clinical and epidemiological research.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the study findings.

claim: Each subsample included around 66% female, with mean age of around 42 years.
source: Each subsample included around 66% female, with mean age of around 42 years.
evidence: This is a description of the sample characteristics.

claim: The NESDA sample consists of 2981 persons between 18 and 65 years including persons with a current or remitted diagnosis of a depressive and/or anxiety disorder (74%) and healthy controls (26%).
source: The NESDA sample consists of 2981 persons between 18 and 65 years including persons with a current or remitted diagnosis of a depressive and/or anxiety disorder (74%) and healthy controls (26%).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample composition.

claim: Individuals were recruited from mental health care settings, general practitioners, and the general population in the period from September 2004 to February 2007.
source: Individuals were recruited from mental health care settings, general practitioners, and the general population in the period from September 2004 to February 2007.
evidence: This is a description of the recruitment methods and timeline.

claim: Persons with insufficient command of the Dutch language or a primary clinical diagnosis of other severe mental disorders were excluded.
source: Persons with insufficient command of the Dutch language or a primary clinical diagnosis of other severe mental disorders, such as severe substance use disorder or a psychotic disorder were excluded.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethical Review Boards of participating centers, and all participants signed informed consent.
source: The study was approved by the Ethical Review Boards of participating centers, and all participants signed informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval and informed consent.

claim: More than 94% of the NESDA participants were from North European origin.
source: More than 94% of the NESDA participants were from North European origin.
evidence: This is a description of the sample demographics.

claim: Leukocyte telomere length was determined using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), adapted from the published original method by Cawthon, 2002.
source: Leukocyte telomere length was determined at the laboratory of Telomere Diagnostics, Inc (Menlo Park, CA, USA), using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), adapted from the published original method by Cawthon, 2002.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for measuring telomere length, supported by a citation.

claim: The intra-assay coefficient of variation for telomere length measurement was 5.1%.
source: The reliability of the assay was adequate: eight included quality control DNA samples on each PCR run illustrated a small intra-assay coefficient of variation (CV = 5.1%), and inter-assay CV was also sufficiently low (CV = 4.6%).
evidence: This is a description of the quality control metrics for the telomere length assay.

claim: The inter-assay coefficient of variation for telomere length measurement was 4.6%.
source: The reliability of the assay was adequate: eight included quality control DNA samples on each PCR run illustrated a small intra-assay coefficient of variation (CV = 5.1%), and inter-assay CV was also sufficiently low (CV = 4.6%).
evidence: This is a description of the quality control metrics for the telomere length assay.

claim: To assay the methylation levels of approximately 28 million common CpG sites in the human genome, an optimized protocol for MBD-seq was used.
source: To assay the methylation levels of the approximately 28 million common CpG sites in the human genome, we used an optimized protocol for MBD-seq (Han et al., 2018; Aberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for DNA methylation measurement, supported by citations.

claim: The optimized MBD-seq protocol assesses about 94% of the CpGs in the methylome.
source: This optimized protocol assesses about 94% of the CpGs in the methylome.
evidence: This is a description of the coverage of the MBD-seq protocol.

claim: Gene expression data were obtained using Affymetrix U219 arrays.
source: Samples were hybridized to Affymetrix U219 arrays (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA).
evidence: This is a description of the platform used for gene expression measurement.

claim: After filtering, data for analysis remained for 423,201 probes, which was summarized into 44,241 probe sets targeting 18,238 genes.
source: After this filtering step, data for analysis remained for 423,201 probes, which was summarized into 44,241 probe sets targeting 18,238 genes.
evidence: This is a description of the gene expression data after quality control.

claim: A panel of 243 analytes was assessed in serum using multiplexed immunoassays.
source: As described previously (Lamers et al., 2016), a panel of 243 analytes (Myriad RBM DiscoveryMAP 250+) involved in various hormonal, immunological, and metabolic pathways was assessed in serum using multiplexed immunoassays in a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)-certified laboratory (Myriad RBM; Austin, TX, USA).
evidence: This is a description of the proteomic measurement methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: After excluding analytes with more than 30% missing data, 171 of the 243 analytes remained for analysis.
source: After excluding analytes with more than 30% missing data (mostly due to values outside the ranges of detection), 171 of the 243 analytes remained for analysis (with values below and above detection limits imputed with the detection limit values).
evidence: This is a description of the data quality control for proteomic measurements.

claim: A total of 232 metabolites or metabolite ratios were reliably quantified using targeted high-throughput proton Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (1H-NMR) metabolomics.
source: In short, a total of 232 metabolites or metabolite ratios were reliably quantified from Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid plasma samples using targeted high-throughput proton Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (1H-NMR) metabolomics (Nightingale Health Ltd, Helsinki, Finland) (Soininen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the metabolomic measurement methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: In total 231 metabolites in 2910 samples remained for analysis after quality control.
source: In total 231 metabolites in 2910 samples remained for analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the final metabolomic dataset after quality control.

claim: For each of the four omics domains, biological age was computed using cross-validation by splitting the sample in 10 equal parts.
source: Finally, biological age was computed using cross-validation by splitting the sample in 10 equal parts.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for computing biological age.

claim: In the training set the biological age estimator was computed using ridge regression with chronological age as the outcome, and the omics data as predictors.
source: In the training set the biological age estimator was computed using ridge regression (R library glmnet), with chronological age as the outcome, and the omics data as predictors.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methodology for building biological clocks.

claim: 80,000 CpGs (mapping to 2976 genes) were selected for the epigenetic clock.
source: This approach resulted in 80,000 CpGs (mapping to 2976 genes) for the epigenetic clock, and 1200 probes (mapping to 767 genes) for the transcriptomic clock.
evidence: This is a description of the number of features used in the epigenetic clock.

claim: 1200 probes (mapping to 767 genes) were selected for the transcriptomic clock.
source: This approach resulted in 80,000 CpGs (mapping to 2976 genes) for the epigenetic clock, and 1200 probes (mapping to 767 genes) for the transcriptomic clock.
evidence: This is a description of the number of features used in the transcriptomic clock.

claim: For the proteomic and metabolomic data, all markers were used to predict age.
source: For the proteomic and metabolomic data, all markers were used to predict age, because leaving markers out decreased the prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is a description of the feature selection approach for proteomic and metabolomic clocks.

claim: Correction for multiple testing was done using permutation based FDR, resulting in a p-value threshold of 2e-2 for an FDR of 5%.
source: Correction for multiple testing was done using permutation based FDR (Fehrmann et al., 2011). Subject labels were permuted 1000 times and associations were computed using the permuted data (all biological aging indicators vs all health determinants). For each of the observed p-values (p) the FDR was computed as the average number of permuted p-values smaller than p, divided by the amount of real p-values smaller than p, resulting in a p-value threshold of 2e-2 for a FDR of 5% for all tests.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methodology for multiple testing correction.

claim: The average chronological age of the cohort was 41 years (sd = 13, range = 18–65 years).
source: The average chronological age of our cohort (mean = 41 years, sd = 13, range = 18–65 years) is rather young, so high rates of mortality and morbidity were not expected.
evidence: This is a description of the sample age characteristics.
